finding.claim: POST /settings/email is guarded by @login_optional instead of @login_required, so the state-changing set_email() runs for unauthenticated callers with g.uid = None. The sibling /settings/password route correctly uses login_required. Impact depends on set_email's implementation (a stub in this file). It could update rows where the user id is NULL, or any 'anonymous' record, or fail with a 500. This is a missing authentication guard on an account-modifying endpoint, and the email change is the usual first step of account takeover through password reset.
finding.source: Unauthenticated HTTP POST to /settings/email with no session cookie
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37, an account email modification

trace.note: login_optional sets g.uid = session.get('uid'), which is None for anonymous callers, and always calls the handler
set_email(None, 'new@example.org') is executed with no authentication or ownership check

finding.guards_checked: login_required is used on /settings/password (line 42) but not here. The handler has no in-body check of g.uid. No other middleware or before_request hook exists in the file. CSRF protection is absent too, but that is not the primary issue.

verdict.guard_found: none (login_optional at routes.py:19-25 only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") and always calls the handler; no in-body check, no before_request hook)
verdict.reason: routes.py:35 applies login_optional (routes.py:22-23), which never aborts, so change_email calls set_email(None, ...) at routes.py:37 for anonymous callers, unlike login_required at routes.py:11-12 on /settings/password; the actual damage depends on set_email, which is only a stub at routes.py:48-49, but the missing authentication guard is real.
